title: How I used AI to ship a hardcore gladiator tactics roguelike as a solo dev (what worked, what didn’t)
author: thvaz
selftext:
I released my first commercial game on Steam a couple of weeks ago: *Chains on Sand*, a very crunchy, tabletop-rpg-ish gladiator roguelike (grid movement, hit locations, limb cripples, crowd system, permadeath, etc.).

I’m a solo dev, and I leaned heavily on generative tools to get it done. Since this sub is about *how* we use AI in game dev, I thought I’d share what actually helped and what I’d avoid next time.

**What I used AI for**

* **Code assistance (ChatGPT)** – prototyping systems like hit-location combat, AI behaviours, save/load, etc. It automated a lot of boilerplate, but bug-fixing and refactors still took a lot of time.
* **Art (mostly Sora)** – backgrounds, UI textures, character concepts. Everything then went through Photoshop by hand. The game uses a modular paperdoll system, so there was a *lot* of cutting, re-layering and editing to make it all work in-game.
* **Music (Suno)** – almost all of the soundtrack was generated with Suno and then curated/edited so it fit the tone of the game.

**What worked well**

* I could iterate on complex systems (active defenses, armor coverage, boss abilities) much faster than if I coded everything from scratch. AI was also great for brainstorming edge cases and ideas — especially useful when you’re a solo dev with nobody to bounce systems off.
* I think I managed to get a coherent and consistent art style for the game despite mixing tools. If you disagree, I’d honestly like to hear why. 🙂
* On a practical level, AI made the difference between “a prototype on my hard drive” and “a finished game with a decent amount of content” (lots of armor/weapons/consumables, multiple bosses, etc.) that I could actually ship.

**What didn’t work / lessons learned**  
• AI art is an instant lightning rod. Many players react to the *label* before they even look at the game.  
• Even with AI, you can’t skip design. If your combat math is off or onboarding is rough, tools won’t save you. 

**Why I’m posting this here**  
I’m not trying to sell “use AI = profit”. I just wanted to give a concrete case from someone who actually shipped something with it: where it helped, where it hurt, and how the launch has been (mixed, but I’m still glad I finished it).

If anyone is curious how this feels as a *player*, the game is [Chains on Sand](https://store.steampowered.com/app/3730720/Chains_on_Sand/). It’s very niche and pretty punishing by design, but I’d especially love feedback from people here who enjoy crunchy tactics games and are interested in AI-assisted workflows.

Happy to answer questions about the pipeline or specific tools I used.

comments.author: mizerr
comments.body: What was your previous game dev experience? And how long did it take you to complete this game?

replies.author: thvaz
replies.body: None. I have a TI background though, It took about a year.

comments.author: bmerrillcreative
comments.body: Congrats on the launch! This looks awesome, appreciate the realistic assessment of AI tools used. Did you use any frameworks for the grid/turn based combat or just author it all yourself with GPT?

replies.author: thvaz
replies.body:
Thanks! It’s built in Unity, but I didn’t use any external frameworks for the tactics side — just Unity’s own grid and tilemap systems as the base.  
The rest (initiative order, movement logic, hit locations, active defenses, etc.) I authored myself with GPT’s help.  
GPT was great for drafting snippets and structure, but I still spent most of the time balancing and debugging manually.

replies.author: bmerrillcreative
replies.body: Awesome makes sense, also embarking on a tile based unity project right now as a solo dev so very encouraging to hear it can be done!

replies.author: thvaz
replies.body: Best of luck on your project!

replies.author: bmerrillcreative
replies.body: Thank you!

replies.author: B-i-g-Boss
replies.body: Did you worked with unity before?

replies.author: thvaz
replies.body: No, this was my first gamedev experience.

replies.author: Failosipher
replies.body: See now that's crazy. That deserves more attention. Congrats btw 👏

comments.author: icekiller333
comments.body:
Congrats :) you took on a larger undertaking and followed through, you should be really proud!

Great breakdown of what worked and didn't.

comments.author: Fun-Marionberry-4867
comments.body: You think the AI label kept away a considerable portion of potential players? Cingratz on the game btw

replies.author: thvaz
replies.body: on Steam didn't got any visible hate, however in other sub I posted (related to the game genre) it seemed I had slaughtered little kittens.

replies.author: Fun-Marionberry-4867
replies.body: Lol ok thanks, have you?..

replies.author: thvaz
replies.body: I should have put the disclaimer: "No kittens were harmed on the making of this game".

comments.author: EverretEvolved
comments.body: How many downloads have you gotten?

replies.author: thvaz
replies.body: I wasn't expecting much but I still got disappointed hahaha. On the steam next fest the demo got around 400 downloads. After launch so far I sold about 50 units. Still have about 1k wishlists though. I guess I lost the right price mark. Not bad for a 0-budget, no marketing project though.

comments.author: Better-Mixture3216
comments.body:
Man i got to say this is inspiring. Im trying alot but with 0 programming skills i just cant make it work. But this gives hope! Looks great, the art is fantastic, like darkest dungeon style. 
This gives me motivation to try again! 
BTW why use gbt and not claude? I find that claude is better for ideas, and hear its considered good coder

replies.author: thvaz
replies.body: Learn a bit of programming logic and you will be ready to go. To be honest never really used Claude. I used a bit of Gemini though.

comments.author: LusikkaFeed
comments.body:
It does kinda look like AI made game in a sense that it looks like what "a videogame" looks to a soulless robot. It does not look fun or interesting at all.

But congrats on shipping a game either way.

replies.author: thvaz
replies.body: Thanks! Totally fair — the game definitely isn’t for everyone, it’s a pretty weird niche project. Appreciate the congrats though.

comments.author: Szabe442
comments.body: Nice job for your first game project. 1k wishlists is pretty great with no marketing. That being said, I think your trailer doesn't do a great job at explaining the complexity of the combat, in fact it makes your game look incredibly simplistic. There is barely anything about loot or the magic system. The art still looks very AI generated and it doesn't feel cohesive, it feels like 2-3 art styles are clashing. I would say the price is too high for a game like this.

replies.author: thvaz
replies.body:
Thanks a lot for the detailed feedback — the trailer note is spot on. Editing trailers is my weakest skill, and this combat relies on a mix of visual cues + combat log, which I didn’t convey well.

I do think the paperdoll art is fairly consistent; where it diverges is some backgrounds/UI and the scroll-style cutscenes (I couldn’t keep that look perfectly uniform). I’ll watch that more closely next time.

About price, you’re right that I missed expectations. It wasn’t greed, more fear of underselling what it is. From your perspective, what price would make you try it?

replies.author: Szabe442
replies.body:
Hm, paperdolls? That doesn't come across at all even when I zoom in. It doesn't seem to have a paper texture.


As for the price, I would say about half of what it is now seems more reasonable, but probably looking at your competition's price range and asking players during playtests is your best bet.

replies.author: thvaz
replies.body: English isn’t my first language. By “paperdolls” I mean the character figures - their appearance changes depending on the equipment they wear.

comments.author: smellysocks234
comments.body: How did you use Sora for backgrounds and textures? I thought Sora is for making videos?

replies.author: thvaz
replies.body: Sora does images also, it is quite good for that even.

comments.author: moneydollarz
comments.body: How did you create the sprite sheet animations? with ai tools? or was it created manually?

replies.author: thvaz
replies.body: The animations are quite simple. Some were just cut from the sprite so they could be moved. Some leg movements were animated on Veo however, then cut and edited on photoshop. So I guess a bit of both.

comments.author: ZombieApoch
comments.body: That’s really impressive, congrats on shipping a full game solo! I like how you used AI as a true helper instead of just relying on it completely. The balance between automation and your own touch comes through. The art and concept sound great too, I’ll definitely check out Chains on Sand. You should try posting it on [vibecodinglist.com](http://vibecodinglist.com) , plenty of devs there would really value your honest insights.

replies.author: thvaz
replies.body: Thanks! I will check it out!

comments.author: Bunnymus-Prime
comments.body: Congratulations, how did you handle marketing and get people to actually buy your game

replies.author: thvaz
replies.body: Well, this is the hard time. It is hard to reach real players. By posting on twitter, reddit, you reach mostly other devs. I managed to get 1000 wishlists but I don't really know how. However, the game is underperforming - it should have sold better with this ammount of wishlists. I didn't expect much though.

comments.author: Cigaro300
comments.body: Thanks for the write up. I'm a solo dev who occasionally asks chat got where a button is or the word of the syntax I'm coding in. It looks like you've done a lot of checking over AIs work or improving it etc. Has that not been a nightmare? Chat gpt whilst extremely powerful nearly always gives me a terrible workaround fix and not intelligent, scalability theory practices. How have you found navigating that?

replies.author: thvaz
replies.body: chatgpt memory is awful, you have to be the memory for it . it understands context well, it just happens that it forgets the context often. So you have to keep the context always fresh to it.

replies.author: Dom_Nation_
replies.body: I just started throwing ideas out there and found the same thing with chat gpt. I've been really happy with claude ai's memory in comparison.
